Nov 12 (Reuters) - Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams and other apps of the company remained disrupted for thousands of users for more than five hours on ‌Thursday, with the outage also hitting connectors used by OpenAI's and Anthropic's ‌AI services. As of 6 p.m. ET, Microsoft said it was still working to return affected servers to service, ​and had observed limited recovery as users gradually reconnected. Reports of Outlook problems peaked at 138,058 around 1 p.m. ET and had fallen to around 34,490 by evening, according to Downdetector. The company had earlier in the day pointed to a number of servers being ‌unexpectedly unavailable for the elevated ⁠load and not an increase in traffic. "We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues ⁠with Exchange Online," a Microsoft spokesperson said. By 5:47 p.m. ET, the number of reports of problems with Microsoft 365 had fallen to nearly 13,000 user, while there were 763 reports ​of users ​having trouble accessing Teams, according to Downdetector. The ​tech giant had then said the ‌restored servers had remained stable so far and that it was shifting traffic to alternate routes wherever possible while streamlining the process to bring the remaining impacted servers back online. "As capacity is restored, users may experience a gradual recovery as their clients reconnect," Microsoft said in a statement. OpenAI said it was investigating an issue ‌with Microsoft connectors in which new connections may ​be broken and tools are not working as ​expected. Anthropic said it had identified an ​issue with an upstream provider affecting its Microsoft 365 connector. Microsoft last ‌month reported an outage of its ​Azure cloud platform that ​impacted the tech giant's suite of productivity software, and a range of industries worldwide. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on ​November 12, rescheduled it to ‌November 16 citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage. title: Microsoft restores services after global Outlook and Teams outage hits more than 130,000 users - Yahoo Finance Australia
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Microsoft says services are returning to normal after a major global outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 products, leaving businesses and users unable to access email and workplace applications. More than 130,000 Outlook outage reports were logged in the United States at the peak of the disruption, while Australia recorded more than 5,500 reports as the problem spread across regions. Microsoft's public service-health page is now showing its products as operational, although the company had earlier said it was still working to accelerate recovery across affected infrastructure. Microsoft traced the disruption to elevated load across part of its infrastructure after a number of servers unexpectedly became unavailable. The company said automated health checks had removed affected servers from service, putting greater pressure on the remaining capacity and causing connectivity errors for Exchange Online users. Microsoft began deploying an alternative health-check method and a targeted change designed to prevent additional servers from being taken offline while engineers restored capacity. The company has not identified a cyberattack as the cause. Outlook users reported being unable to send or receive emails, access inboxes or connect through web and desktop applications. Teams, Copilot, OneDrive and some Azure services also experienced increased error reports during the outage. Microsoft said an earlier Teams issue in North America had been restored separately, although some users continued to report intermittent problems during the wider Microsoft 365 disruption. The outage again highlights the dependence of businesses, governments and remote workers on a small number of major cloud platforms. With Microsoft 365 deeply embedded across corporate email, collaboration, storage and AI tools, failures in shared infrastructure can rapidly spread across multiple services and regions. For Australian organisations, the incident is another reminder of the operational risk created by concentrating critical communications and productivity systems within a single cloud ecosystem. title: Widespread Microsoft outage takes down Outlook and other 365 services - CNBC
content:
Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday that impacted thousands of users across regions, according to outage-tracking website Downdetector.com. The outage began shortly before 1 p.m. and impacted Microsoft 365 services, Outlook and Teams. At the time, about 130,000 users reported issues with Outlook. Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site. “We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online,” a Microsoft spokesperson wrote in a statement to CNBC. “We appreciate our customers’ patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible.” Microsoft shared updates on the outage from its Microsoft 365 Status account on social media platform X. Amazon wrote on X that services were “operating normally” and an “unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports.” The company referred users to its health dashboard for “accurate data.” At 4 p.m., Microsoft said it had “validated an alternative service health check method” that brought some affected servers back online. “We’re now applying this change more broadly,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses.” Microsoft initially said infrastructure “elevated load across multiple regions” was responsible for the connectivity problems. The company later determined that the elevated load was caused by a “number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure” and that some servers were failing automated health checks. “We’ve taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service,” Microsoft wrote. title: MSFT Stock Reverses and Heads to $500 After Microsoft 365 Services Impacted by Outlook Outage - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft shares retreat toward $520 after a service disruption affects Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Microsoft 365, adding another source of uncertainty as investors reassess rising infrastructure costs, competition from Anthropic and the profitability of cloud expansion. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have extended their retreat from record highs near $560, falling toward $520 as investors confront another setback for the technology giant. The stock had recovered sharply from the $500 area following the U.S. midterm elections, but renewed concerns about infrastructure spending, competition and operational reliability have weakened sentiment. Thursday’s decline accelerated after disruptions affected several Microsoft services, including Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Microsoft 365. Users reported difficulties accessing email, workplace collaboration tools and other cloud-based applications, while Microsoft warned that the disruption could affect service connectivity across multiple regions. Downdetector recorded more than 130,000 reports of Outlook problems at 1:27 p.m. ET, alongside more than 46,000 reports involving Microsoft 365 and approximately 3,000 concerning Teams. These figures represent user-submitted reports rather than confirmed numbers of affected customers. Microsoft initially said it had resolved a Teams disruption affecting North American users, but subsequently indicated that the wider connectivity issue could affect Microsoft 365 customers internationally. Although temporary service disruptions do not necessarily indicate a structural problem, the incident highlights the dependence of businesses on Microsoft’s cloud-based productivity ecosystem. The outage comes as Microsoft faces growing scrutiny over the cost and scale of its infrastructure expansion. Noelle Walsh, President of Cloud Operations and Innovation, reiterated that Microsoft would finance its own data-centre construction and associated infrastructure. Her comments extend a community-first commitment announced in January 2026, under which the company pledged to cover electricity costs and grid upgrades associated with its projects rather than transferring those expenses to local residents. Walsh oversees Microsoft’s global data-centre operations, managing approximately 15,000 employees and a multibillion-dollar investment programme. While covering infrastructure costs could reduce community opposition and regulatory friction, it also reinforces the financial burden associated with expanding Azure and computing capacity. Investors increasingly want evidence that additional infrastructure can generate sufficient revenue without weakening margins and free cash flow. Competition is another emerging concern after Anthropic introduced workplace software targeting markets dominated by Microsoft and Google. Its products include a videoconferencing assistant, data dashboards and Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet service positioned against Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. The company also plans to allow enterprises to integrate existing applications into Claude, potentially turning the platform into a central interface for workplace activities. This represents a competitive challenge for Microsoft’s productivity ecosystem. Microsoft 365 Cloud generated $27.78 billion in first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue, ended September 30, 2026, increasing approximately 17% year-over-year and accounting for around 30% of total company revenue. Although this includes broader commercial and consumer cloud services, it demonstrates the importance of the productivity business to Microsoft’s financial performance. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MSFT buyers gave up at this zone, reversing lower below $520 today. Microsoft’s latest quarterly results remained impressive. Net income increased 32% year-over-year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, while revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year-over-year, or 31% in constant currency. However, strong earnings have not eliminated concerns about the capital required to maintain growth. Data centres, servers, networking equipment and specialised processors require substantial upfront investment, and investors increasingly want measurable returns rather than larger spending commitments. An amended filing concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions. Microsoft is also developing its Maia 300 custom processor, reportedly targeting 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems. Its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to improve rack-scale computing capacity. Custom silicon could eventually reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers, but development and deployment require additional investment before those efficiency gains translate into stronger profitability. Microsoft’s latest retreat reflects several overlapping concerns: service reliability, rising infrastructure costs, Anthropic’s competitive expansion and questions about future returns. The company’s strong earnings and cloud growth remain important positives, but investors are becoming increasingly selective about the financial benefits of expanding computing capacity. With MSFT retreating from $560 toward $520, the immediate technical focus shifts to whether buyers can defend the $520 area. A sustained recovery will require renewed buying interest and stronger confidence that Microsoft’s infrastructure investments can deliver profitable growth without undermining free cash flow.

title: Morgan Stanley previews next week's Microsoft (MSFT.US) Ignite conference: The "enterprise AI flywheel" faces a critical test, with five key focal points. - 富途牛牛
content: Microsoft's Ignite conference opens next week, and Morgan Stanley treats it as a review rather than a launch event. The Zhitong Finance APP has learned that Microsoft (MSFT.US)'s Ignite conference opens next week, and Morgan Stanley views it as a validation event rather than a launch event. In a forward-looking report released on Thursday, the firm maintained an "Overweight" rating and a $650 price target. The report's focus is not on new products, but on whether a closed loop can be proven to have been established: Azure provides computing power, Fabric offers an enterprise context, Foundry orchestrates models and agents, and M365 together with Copilot integrates intelligence into employees' daily workflows. Morgan Stanley refers to these four layers as the "Enterprise AI Flywheel" and believes Ignite's value lies in demonstrating that it is translating into broader production deployments and higher full-stack consumption. The conference will be held in San Francisco from November 17 to 20. The core session is scheduled for 1 p.m. EST on November 17 (2 a.m. Beijing time on November 18), followed by a sell-side Q&A with CEO Satya Nadella at 4 p.m.; on November 18 at 3 p.m., Morgan Stanley will meet with CFO Amy Hood and Vice President of Investor Relations Jonathan Neilson. The foundation is solid, but we need to clearly explain what makes it so. The report is based on the first fiscal quarter of 2027, released on October 28. Revenue for the quarter reached $92.3 billion, up 19% year over year; Azure grew 48% (at constant currency, accelerating 6 percentage points sequentially), and M365 commercial cloud accelerated to 18% (at constant currency). Operating margin was approximately 50%. According to Morgan Stanley, this mix supports its view of revenue growth "remaining in the high teens and accelerating toward the low 20s," as well as profit growth above 20%. However, Azure's 48% growth rate warrants a closer look: both the enterprise and small-to-medium business segments are strengthening simultaneously, driven by core cloud services and AI infrastructure together—not by any single customer type. Commercial remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached $677 billion, up 73% year over year, with roughly 30% expected to convert within the next 12 months. This provides strong revenue visibility and underpins management's confidence to continue increasing capital expenditures. Morgan Stanley has identified five key observations for this conference, which essentially represent a deconstruction of its "flywheel": First, Copilot's next frontier is ARPU, not seat count. The report's three-pillar thesis is: direct seat penetration, migration to E7 plans, and usage-based billing. The significance of the third pillar is that it can expand Microsoft's revenue boundaries from "software budgets" to "budgets for knowledge work and business processes." The two figures cited in the report are: Copilot's daily active users increased by approximately 50% quarter-over-quarter, and customers actively consuming credits increased by over 75% quarter-over-quarter. Second, Foundry's value has shifted from "providing you with models" to "managing how you use the models." In the first fiscal quarter, Foundry revenue more than tripled year over year, and the number of customers building multi-model agentic solutions increased fivefold year over year. Based on this, Morgan Stanley believes that greater model diversity is a boon rather than a burden for Microsoft—because the more customers switch among multiple models, the more they need a unified orchestration layer. Third, Fabric operates within an "enterprise context." As the underlying model itself becomes a commodity, governed enterprise data and context become the sources of differentiation. In the first fiscal quarter, more than 19,000 customers used both Fabric and Foundry, up from just over 17,000 last quarter. While the growth rate isn't rapid, it signals that customers are willing to bring their data onto the platform. Fourth, the widespread adoption of proxies is turning security into an entry point. As proxies begin accessing corporate data and performing actions across applications, customers must manage their identities, permissions, and behaviors. Consequently, the relevance of Entra, Defender, and Purview increases, further justifying the upgrade path from M365 to E5/E7. Agent 365, unveiled at Ignite last year, marks the starting point of this trajectory. Fifth, the Maia 300 is a variable on the cost curve. As long as demand continues to exceed supply, the deployment roadmap for in-house chips, the workloads they support, and their cost advantage relative to third-party solutions will be key to determining whether Azure's product‑level gross margin can improve. Gross margins are trending lower, but that's not the whole story. Improvements at the Azure product level partially offset the structural pressure from the rising share of Azure revenue; more importantly, the additional capacity freed up through efficiency gains was allocated to Foundry and quickly monetized—thereby supporting both revenue growth and operating leverage. According to Morgan Stanley's model, the trajectory of this curve is clear: gross margin declines from 67.9% in fiscal year 2026 to 65.9% in fiscal year 2027, 64.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 63.5% in fiscal year 2029, while operating margin remains virtually unchanged—46.8%, 46.6%, 46.7%, and 47.2%. In other words, the erosion in gross margin is offset by operating leverage—this is the key to whether this round of AI-related spending can be tolerated: the market will accept a decline in gross margin only if operating margin holds steady. The $650 base-case scenario corresponds to about 26 times FY2028 EPS of $24.41. On a reported basis, 26 times is a slight premium to large-cap software peers, and a 1.2x PEG ratio is below Microsoft's historical level and that of its peers. In the bull case, at $800, this implies roughly 29 times, or $27.41; in the bear case, at $300, it implies $22.25. The probabilities derived from implied volatility of options are: approximately 23.0% of reaching above $650, about 6.1% of reaching above $800, and roughly 6.8% of falling below $300. There is virtually no disagreement in the sell-side consensus: 97% overweight, 3% neutral, and 0% underweight. This forward-looking blind spot happens to be the one the market cares about most this week: Microsoft has stopped disclosing the number of paid Copilot seats. For the three consecutive quarters prior, paid seats (which last exceeded 30 million in disclosures) were the most direct metric for outsiders to gauge the progress of its AI implementation. However, this figure disappeared from the first fiscal quarter's earnings press release and conference call. Chief Financial Officer Hood told analysts that "no update on Copilot numbers was disclosed" this quarter, instead pointing to "momentum in revenue and usage." Nadella cited a "nearly 50% quarter-over-quarter increase" in daily active users and a "more than 75% quarter-over-quarter increase" in customers consuming credits, neither of which provided any baseline figures. This coincides with Microsoft's shift in pricing. The $99 M365 E7 suite and Agent 365 have already pushed customers toward a hybrid "seat fee + metered" model; Copilot Business, sold through the cloud solution provider channel, defaults to usage-based billing for new purchases and imposes a cap of 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month—arrangements originally scheduled to take effect on December 1 were postponed to January–March 2027 following partner feedback. Morgan Stanley cites "50% increase in daily active users" as evidence of demand, but without access to the underlying seat numbers, the true significance of these percentages hinges on what their denominators actually represent. Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, told the media that many organizations are "still trying to figure out exactly what this Copilot is useful for"—whether it serves as "a fancy search tool" or as an agent integrated into workflows. This very question is precisely what Ignite must address—and Morgan Stanley assumes it already has. Two conditions that must both be true simultaneously The report's logic hinges on two conditions being met simultaneously: revenue must keep pace with rising consumption after Copilot switches to a pay-as-you-go model, and capital expenditure intensity must stop increasing. Capital spending in the first fiscal quarter was $45.2 billion (including finance leases), while the company guides for over $50 billion in the second fiscal quarter and approximately $170 billion for the full fiscal year 2027; free cash flow stood at $18.6 billion, down 27% year over year, making it the only one of the three major cloud providers still posting positive free cash flow. So at Ignite, what's truly worth listening to isn't how many agent templates were announced, but three key questions: how Copilot will be priced on a metered basis; whether Foundry can maintain its position in the orchestration layer within a multi‑model world; and whether its in‑house chips can drive down the cost per unit of compute. The first two determine the revenue ceiling, while the third sets the profit floor. In another report, Citi set a price target of $680 and assigned a "buy" rating, with reasoning similar to this report: Following a strong first fiscal quarter, Azure has reached an inflection point, and the conference will focus on infrastructure, proprietary cutting-edge models, Foundry, and the Copilot+IQ strategy. title: MSFT Stock Heads to $500 as Microsoft Data-Centre Spending and Anthropic Workplace Competition Intensify - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft stock retreat from the record high near $560 as renewed data-centre spending commitments, competition from Anthropic’s workplace software and questions about future infrastructure returns weigh on investor sentiment. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have reversed their recent rally, falling more than 2.5% toward $520 after approaching $560 last week. The decline follows a strong recovery from the $500 area, supported by improving sentiment across technology stocks after the U.S. midterm elections. However, enthusiasm is fading as investors reassess the costs of expanding cloud infrastructure and the returns expected from massive computing commitments. Fresh pressure emerged after Noelle Walsh, Microsoft’s President of Cloud Operations and Innovation, reiterated that the company would pay for its own data-centre construction and associated infrastructure. The commitment comes as communities increasingly question who should cover the electricity networks, power lines, substations and utility upgrades required by large data-centre developments. Walsh oversees Microsoft’s global data-centre operations, managing approximately 15,000 employees and a multibillion-dollar investment programme. Her comments extend a community-first commitment announced in January 2026, under which Microsoft pledged to cover electricity costs and grid infrastructure upgrades associated with its projects rather than passing those expenses on to local residents. The company operates hundreds of facilities supporting Azure and its expanding computing workloads. Although taking responsibility for infrastructure costs could help reduce community opposition and regulatory friction, it also reinforces the financial burden associated with Microsoft’s expansion strategy. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the revenue generated by additional computing capacity will justify the substantial investment required to build and operate these facilities. Competition is another emerging concern after Anthropic introduced a new suite of workplace software targeting markets dominated by Microsoft and Google. The products include a videoconferencing assistant, data dashboards and Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet service positioned against Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. Several tools are reportedly available in beta to paying customers. More importantly, Anthropic plans to allow enterprises to integrate existing applications into Claude, potentially positioning its platform as a central interface for workplace activities rather than simply an assistant operating alongside traditional software. This creates a competitive challenge for Microsoft’s productivity ecosystem. Microsoft 365 Cloud generated $27.78 billion in revenue during the first quarter of fiscal 2027, ended September 30, 2026, representing approximately 17% year-over-year growth and around 30% of total company revenue. While this figure covers the broader productivity cloud business rather than Excel alone, it illustrates the importance of the segment to Microsoft’s financial performance. Microsoft’s latest quarterly results remained impressive. Net income increased 32% year-over-year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, comfortably exceeding expectations, while earnings surpassed the analyst consensus of $4.27 per share. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year-over-year, or 31% in constant currency. CEO Satya Nadella highlighted improvements in computing capacity, customer choice, security and cost efficiency. Nevertheless, strong earnings have not removed concerns about capital expenditure, particularly as data centres, servers, networking equipment and specialised processors require enormous upfront investment. Investors increasingly want evidence that cloud growth can translate into sustainable profitability without weakening margins and free cash flow. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MSFT buyers gave up at this zone, reversing lower below $520 today. An amended filing concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions. While the arrangement highlights substantial future computing demand, it also raises questions about the financial obligations required to support expanding infrastructure capacity. Microsoft is attempting to improve those economics through its own silicon development. Its Maia 300 processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver significantly higher rack-scale throughput than Maia 200. Custom processors could eventually reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers. However, development and deployment require additional investment before those efficiency improvements translate into stronger returns. Microsoft’s consumer businesses offer a less encouraging picture. The Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion in revenue, down 3% year-over-year. Search and advertising revenue increased 12%, but Xbox content and services declined 2%, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue dropped 22%. Regulatory pressure is another consideration. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority has proposed designating Microsoft as having strategic market status in certain software markets, potentially increasing scrutiny of licensing, pricing and product bundling. For MSFT investors, the challenge is becoming increasingly clear: Microsoft continues to deliver strong revenue and earnings growth, but the cost of maintaining its competitive position is rising. With shares retreating from $560 toward $520, investors may demand stronger evidence that infrastructure expansion and future computing commitments can generate sufficient returns to justify current valuations.

title: Anthropic Now Makes Its Own Spreadsheet Software. Here's What I'd Do With Microsoft Stock. - The Motley Fool
content: Claude Sheets is still in beta. Should the Excel maker's shareholders worry? Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) firm behind the Claude chatbot, now has a spreadsheet of its own. On Tuesday, Nov. 10, it released Claude Sheets and Claude Whiteboards in beta, and made its dashboard tool generally available under a new name, Claude Data. This gives Claude an alternative to Excel. Microsoft (MSFT +0.36%) sells Excel as part of Microsoft 365, a business that pulled in about $111 billion in revenue for the software giant's fiscal 2026, which ended June 30. Microsoft shares dropped 2.2% on Tuesday, to roughly $533, but they're still up about 10% this year as I write. I don't think a beta spreadsheet is a reason to sell the stock. But the launch is a good excuse to look at the business it overlaps with -- and one number in it that's been cooling. According to Anthropic's launch post, Claude Sheets can make a spreadsheet with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-down menus, often from one prompt. Claude changes the cells directly, and colleagues can work on the same sheet together. Anthropic is open about the limits, though. Its post says the sheets have "simple spreadsheet functionality" for now. And for anyone who needs everything Excel can do, it suggests exporting the file to .xlsx or CSV, or using Claude for Excel, which works in Microsoft's own spreadsheet. The rollout to big companies is cautious, too. Sheets and Whiteboards are on by default for Team plans but off by default for Enterprise customers. Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. That might change as Anthropic adds features. But companies typically get Excel as part of Microsoft 365, a subscription that also includes email, Teams, file storage, and security tools. A better spreadsheet alone wouldn't replace all of that. Microsoft 365's commercial and consumer businesses brought in around a third of the $332 billion of revenue Microsoft reported for fiscal 2026. Profit's tougher to nail down, because Microsoft now reports Microsoft 365 in a new agents and infra segment that also covers Azure, its cloud computing platform. Under the old setup, though, the productivity and business processes segment (Microsoft 365 plus LinkedIn and Dynamics) made $83.9 billion in operating income in fiscal 2026, up 20% from a year earlier. This was around 54% of the company's total, making it Microsoft's most profitable segment by a big margin. And the business keeps growing fast. In the fiscal first quarter of 2027 (from July through September 2026), Microsoft 365 cloud revenue rose 17% year over year to $27.8 billion, or around 30% of total revenue. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue also grew 17%, near the 16% to 20% pace it kept through fiscal 2026. Plus, management sees around 19% growth in constant currency (leaving out exchange-rate moves) this quarter, with growth picking up through the year. The number to watch is seats. Growth in paid Microsoft 365 commercial seats was 6% to 7% year over year in each of the four quarters of fiscal 2026. In the fiscal first quarter, it slowed to 5%. In other words, more of Microsoft's growth is coming from charging each user more. Revenue per user climbed on upgrades to premium plans, such as Microsoft 365 Copilot (its AI assistant for work) and the E5 and E7 bundles. CFO Amy Hood linked some of the seat slowdown to "weaker sales execution" in Microsoft's standard E3 plan and stand-alone products on the Oct. 28 earnings call. Notably, the quarter closed weeks before Claude Sheets arrived, so the release wasn't behind it. Still, if a rival tool starts winning over Microsoft's customers, seat growth is likely where it'd turn up first. Microsoft reported $18.04 per share over the past four quarters on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis, excluding gains and losses from its OpenAI stake. At roughly $533, that's about 30 times adjusted earnings. Adjusted earnings per share climbed 18% year over year last quarter, so this isn't an excessively high price. But it doesn't leave much room for seat growth to keep sliding. For investors who already hold Microsoft, I don't see a reason to sell over a spreadsheet that steers its heaviest users back to Excel. For new money, though, I think the stock's a little too pricey here. title: February 2027 Microsoft Entra MFA Deadline Pushes Soprano Design (MSFT +2.74%) To Launch SMS And Voice Authentication Bridge - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 11, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis A hard deadline is concentrating minds across enterprise IT departments, with Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) set to retire SMS and Voice delivery inside Microsoft Entra ID from February 1, 2027. The move is part of a broader shift by the technology giant toward passkeys as its preferred default authentication experience for users. Organisations that still depend on telephony-based multi-factor authentication will be required to source and manage their own third-party providers once Microsoft withdraws the built-in capability. Sydney-based Soprano Design, which powers more than 32 billion secure interactions annually across 4,500-plus organisations, has stepped into that gap with a dedicated integration product. The company has launched Soprano Connect for Microsoft Entra, making it available through the Microsoft Security Store under both per-user and per-transaction pricing structures. Soprano has held Microsoft partner status for more than 15 years, giving it an established position from which to serve enterprise and government clients affected by the upcoming retirement. Chief Technology Officer Mohamed Odah framed the challenge as one of balancing progress with operational continuity, saying: “Having provided secure authentication solutions to our enterprise and government customers for more than 30 years, we understand that organisations must balance the adoption of new authentication methods with continuity for the users, systems and requirements they support today.” Director of Product and Development Asha Potla cautioned against underestimating the complexity involved, noting that “for many organisations, this won’t be a simple switch from one authentication method to another.” Potla added that varying regulatory requirements, user groups, and system dependencies can create sharply different authentication needs even within a single organisation, and that early planning is critical. Microsoft’s own partner product manager for security, Ankur Patel, endorsed the integration’s rationale directly, stating: “Security continuity is key to our ecosystem. As we evolve our authentication practices, we want customers to have clear options that meet their business needs.” Patel went further, noting that Soprano’s connection to Microsoft Entra ID workforce tenants gives clients “the flexibility to choose the telephony provider that best supports their users and organizational requirements.” The product is specifically targeted at businesses with regulatory, technical, or operational mandates that prevent a clean migration away from SMS or Voice MFA before the retirement rollout begins. Soprano Design operates globally from its Sydney headquarters and serves clients across healthcare, finance, logistics, and government sectors, markets where authentication continuity carries significant compliance weight. title: Microsoft (MSFT) Is Getting Paid for AI Agents. That’s Why I’m Bullish - The Globe and Mail
content: Microsoft (MSFT) is getting paid for artificial intelligence (AI) agents, software that can finish tasks on its own. The maker of Windows and Microsoft 365 now charges more and more customers for how much work these agents do. This makes me bullish on Microsoft. Its AI push is starting to pay for itself, and the company keeps very high margins even while it spends heavily on data centers. The latest quarter backs that up. Revenue from Azure, Microsoft’s cloud platform, grew 48%. The operating margin, the share of sales left after operating costs, reached about 50%. The stock is up 9.7% this year. It is no longer cheap after its rally since June, and AI spending keeps climbing. However, I believe agents give Microsoft a clear way to earn that money back. Microsoft gets paid for AI agents mostly through usage. Copilot, its AI assistant, has mainly been sold as a monthly per-user license, but customers can now also buy credits and pay for the work their agents do. Copilot customers using these credits grew more than 75% in a single quarter, while paid Microsoft 365 commercial seats rose just 5% year-over-year. The two figures measure different things, but the difference in pace stands out. License sales follow a customer’s headcount, while credit sales follow the work agents take on, which can grow much faster. Agent 365, Microsoft’s registry for managing a company’s agents, now holds more than 50 million agents, up over 30% in one quarter. Foundry, where companies build their own AI apps and agents, passed 120,000 customers, and its revenue more than tripled year-over-year. I think Copilot is a big part of Microsoft’s future, because usage keeps climbing. Daily users grew more than fivefold year-over-year, and user satisfaction is at an all-time high. Big companies are buying in, too. The number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats grew more than eightfold in a year, and Volkswagen (VWAGY) has rolled out Copilot to more than 330,000 employees. For Microsoft, more usage now means more revenue. Azure keeps speeding up, and agents are part of the reason, since they need a lot of computing power. Its revenue grew 48% in the September quarter, ahead of what Wall Street expected, helped by Foundry. Management expects 49% to 50% growth in the December quarter, excluding currency effects. Microsoft is also getting more out of its hardware. Copilot workload throughput, meaning how much AI work its systems can process, rose more than 50% in one quarter, which should make each AI task cheaper to run. Microsoft’s AI spending is high, but I think it is manageable. The company spent $135.9 billion on capex over the past four quarters, mostly on data centers and chips, and that number is still rising. The risk of overinvesting will always be there. That is why return on invested capital (ROIC) is the number I watch most closely. It shows how much profit a company makes on the money put into its business. Adding up the last four quarters gives Microsoft an ROIC of about 22%, so it earns roughly 22 cents on every dollar invested. That is slightly lower than a year earlier, but returns have improved in each of the last two quarters, so I don’t see a red flag during such a big build-out. Microsoft is also careful with cash. Over the past 12 months, it still had about $60 billion of free cash flow, the money left after capex. I usually prefer companies that spend more aggressively, but I understand why Microsoft doesn’t want to make its shareholders nervous. In late October, it raised $25 billion in its first major U.S. bond sale since 2017, which gives it more room to keep building data centers without draining its own cash. Management expects free cash flow to stay positive in Fiscal 2027 and says it is confident these investments will pay off over the long run. That convinces me, because agents are already turning part of this spending into revenue. Microsoft stock isn’t too expensive, in my view, although it is no longer cheap. Its trailing-12-month (TTM) price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is around 27.7x, based on reported profit, so investors pay about $27.7 for each dollar Microsoft earns in a year. That is higher than the 20.72x it traded at when Fiscal 2026 ended in June, after a sharp sell-off in the first half of the year. Still, it is well below the levels of the three fiscal years before that, when the P/E ended each year above 35x. Looking at the next 12 months, the forward P/E is about 26x, based on analysts’ estimates of adjusted earnings, which leave out the impact of Microsoft’s investment in OpenAI. I think 26x is a fair price for a company that keeps about half of its sales as operating profit. The main risk is margins. Microsoft’s cloud gross margin, the share of cloud revenue left after the direct cost of running it, is already shrinking as lower-margin Azure makes up a bigger part of cloud sales. Management also expects operating margin to dip slightly from a year earlier in the December quarter. If that continues, the stock will start to look expensive. Wall Street sees Microsoft very positively, with a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 35 Buys, four Holds, and zero Sells assigned in the last three months. At $632.48, the average Microsoft price target implies 16.01% upside potential. Bernstein analyst Mark Moerdler, one of the top analysts on TipRanks, raised his price target to $722 from $662 after the September-quarter report and reiterated his Outperform (Buy) rating on November 6, implying about 32% upside. He believes lower-than-expected capex and capacity delays created some unwarranted noise around solid results, and I fully agree. I’m bullish on Microsoft. It is spending a lot on AI, and I can already see how that money comes back through agents that customers pay for as they use them. The next test is keeping returns this high while the build-out continues. So far, Microsoft is passing it. © Copyright 2026 The Globe and Mail Inc. All rights reserved.

Its fiscal first-quarter report on October 28, 2026, is a fair moment to check that picture, because management said on that call it will access additional sources of funding when it believes doing so is attractive. So what has actually shifted inside the business you own? Microsoft Now Reinvests Far More Of Each Sales Dollar Over the twelve months to September 2026, Microsoft’s capital spending reached 39.2% of its revenue. That figure compares with a median of 10.7% over the 52 quarter ends from December 2012 to September 2025. This heavier spending leaves the company with less surplus cash. Free cash flow, the cash Microsoft retains after that spending, accounted for 17.3% of revenue over the same twelve months, compared with a median of 29.5% in those earlier years. The latest quarter reflects the same shift. During fiscal Q1 2027, free cash flow fell to $18.6 billion from $25.7 billion a year earlier, even though revenue grew. Microsoft is not generating less cash, since cash from operations kept rising over the twelve months. The company is funneling far more of that cash back into the business. According to management on the October 28 call, Microsoft is spending more because demand for its cloud capacity is running ahead of what the company has. Executives said that accelerating demand led the company to add 24 new data centers in the quarter, and that customer demand continues to exceed available supply. This demand is visible within the cloud business itself. Revenue from Azure, Microsoft’s cloud platform, increased 48% in fiscal Q1 2027, a pace management said was ahead of expectations. Microsoft still funds its dividends and buybacks out of free cash flow, but the company operates with far less to spare. Over the twelve months to September 2026, Microsoft paid $48.0 billion in dividends and buybacks out of $60.0 billion of free cash flow. A year earlier, it paid $44.7 billion out of $78.0 billion. The company’s cash pile has shrunk as well. Cash and short-term investments fell to $64.3 billion at the end of September 2026, down from $102 billion a year earlier. This total remains higher than Microsoft’s $57.2 billion of debt, so the company continues to hold net cash. Here is news a holder can like: debt was 7.3% of Microsoft’s assets at the end of September 2026, against a median of 19.0% from December 2012 to September 2025. With so little debt, Microsoft has room to borrow, and after the call it expected to raise $25 billion in a U.S. bond sale. Management expects the spending to keep rising, to over $50 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, against $45.2 billion in the first quarter. That $45.2 billion counts finance leases when they begin; the cash Microsoft paid for property and equipment was $39.4 billion. Historically, a Microsoft shareholder could assume a large share of every sales dollar would return as spare cash, leaving plenty left over after the dividend and the buyback. That dynamic no longer holds. The spending pays off for investors only if Microsoft turns its new capacity into revenue, and management said each dollar of capital spending has the potential to support more revenue and higher returns over time. When the company reports again, expected in January 2027, the figures to watch will be Microsoft’s capital spending against its revenue and the free cash flow left after it. content: Part 2 of 3 on Microsoft and AI. Start with part 1: How Microsoft Missed $2 Trillion In AI. Open Outlook in the morning. The AI that summarizes your inbox might be OpenAI’s, or Anthropic’s, or Microsoft’s own. You don’t care, and neither does your IT department’s bill: it goes to Microsoft either way. That’s the case for Microsoft in one sentence. It doesn’t need the best model if it owns the place where you use one. The case against is just as simple. If the model does the real work, writing the deck, building the spreadsheet, answering the email, then whoever owns it can raise the price, and Microsoft becomes a middleman paying a supplier. Either way, you probably own both sides: the landlord in Microsoft, the model makers through Google and Amazon. In a portfolio of a few million dollars, which side is bigger? Microsoft (MSFT) is getting paid for artificial intelligence (AI) agents, software that can finish tasks on its own. The maker of Windows and Microsoft 365 now charges more and more customers for how much work these agents do. This makes me bullish on Microsoft. Its AI push is starting to pay for itself, and the company keeps very high margins even while it spends heavily on data centers. The latest quarter backs that up. Revenue from Azure, Microsoft's cloud platform, grew 48%. The operating margin, the share of sales left after operating costs, reached about 50%. The stock is up 9.7% this year. It is no longer cheap after its rally since June, and AI spending keeps climbing. However, I believe agents give Microsoft a clear way to earn that money back. Microsoft gets paid for AI agents mostly through usage. Copilot, its AI assistant, has mainly been sold as a monthly per-user license, but customers can now also buy credits and pay for the work their agents do. Copilot customers using these credits grew more than 75% in a single quarter, while paid Microsoft 365 commercial seats rose just 5% year-over-year. Get 75% Off TipRanks Premium and unlock powerful investing tools to make smarter, more confident investment decisions Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks The two figures measure different things, but the difference in pace stands out. License sales follow a customer's headcount, while credit sales follow the work agents take on, which can grow much faster. Agent 365, Microsoft's registry for managing a company's agents, now holds more than 50 million agents, up over 30% in one quarter. Foundry, where companies build their own AI apps and agents, passed 120,000 customers, and its revenue more than tripled year-over-year. I think Copilot is a big part of Microsoft's future, because usage keeps climbing. Daily users grew more than fivefold year-over-year, and user satisfaction is at an all-time high. Big companies are buying in, too. The number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats grew more than eightfold in a year, and Volkswagen (VWAGY) has rolled out Copilot to more than 330,000 employees. For Microsoft, more usage now means more revenue. Azure keeps speeding up, and agents are part of the reason, since they need a lot of computing power. Its revenue grew 48% in the September quarter, ahead of what Wall Street expected, helped by Foundry. Management expects 49% to 50% growth in the December quarter, excluding currency effects. Microsoft is also getting more out of its hardware. Copilot workload throughput, meaning how much AI work its systems can process, rose more than 50% in one quarter, which should make each AI task cheaper to run. Microsoft's AI spending is high, but I think it is manageable. The company spent $135.9 billion on capex over the past four quarters, mostly on data centers and chips, and that number is still rising. The risk of overinvesting will always be there. That is why return on invested capital (ROIC) is the number I watch most closely. It shows how much profit a company makes on the money put into its business. Adding up the last four quarters gives Microsoft an ROIC of about 22%, so it earns roughly 22 cents on every dollar invested. That is slightly lower than a year earlier, but returns have improved in each of the last two quarters, so I don't see a red flag during such a big build-out. Microsoft is also careful with cash. Over the past 12 months, it still had about $60 billion of free cash flow, the money left after capex. I usually prefer companies that spend more aggressively, but I understand why Microsoft doesn't want to make its shareholders nervous. In late October, it raised $25 billion in its first major U.S. bond sale since 2017, which gives it more room to keep building data centers without draining its own cash. Management expects free cash flow to stay positive in Fiscal 2027 and says it is confident these investments will pay off over the long run. That convinces me, because agents are already turning part of this spending into revenue. Microsoft stock isn't too expensive, in my view, although it is no longer cheap. Its trailing-12-month (TTM) price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is around 27.7x, based on reported profit, so investors pay about $27.7 for each dollar Microsoft earns in a year. That is higher than the 20.72x it traded at when Fiscal 2026 ended in June, after a sharp sell-off in the first half of the year. Still, it is well below the levels of the three fiscal years before that, when the P/E ended each year above 35x. Looking at the next 12 months, the forward P/E is about 26x, based on analysts' estimates of adjusted earnings, which leave out the impact of Microsoft's investment in OpenAI. I think 26x is a fair price for a company that keeps about half of its sales as operating profit. The main risk is margins. Microsoft's cloud gross margin, the share of cloud revenue left after the direct cost of running it, is already shrinking as lower-margin Azure makes up a bigger part of cloud sales. Management also expects operating margin to dip slightly from a year earlier in the December quarter. If that continues, the stock will start to look expensive. Wall Street sees Microsoft very positively, with a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 35 Buys, four Holds, and zero Sells assigned in the last three months. At $632.48, the average Microsoft price target implies 16.01% upside potential. Bernstein analyst Mark Moerdler, one of the top analysts on TipRanks, raised his price target to $722 from $662 after the September-quarter report and reiterated his Outperform (Buy) rating on November 6, implying about 32% upside. He believes lower-than-expected capex and capacity delays created some unwarranted noise around solid results, and I fully agree. I'm bullish on Microsoft. It is spending a lot on AI, and I can already see how that money comes back through agents that customers pay for as they use them. The next test is keeping returns this high while the build-out continues. So far, Microsoft is passing it. Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results

title: Microsoft MSFT Stock Drops From $560 on Excel Challenge Following Anthropic Workplace Software Announcement - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft stock retreated from the record high after Anthropic unveiled new workplace software, intensifying competition for Microsoft 365 while investors continue to assess infrastructure spending, future computing commitments and the profitability of cloud expansion. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares rallied sharply last week, recovering from a decline toward $500 to approach $560 and establish a new record high. Improving sentiment across technology stocks following the U.S. midterm elections helped attract buyers, despite growing concerns about data-centre spending, financing requirements and the returns on massive computing investments. However, the recovery has lost momentum this week. Microsoft shares dropped more than 3% to $530.39 following Anthropic’s announcement of new workplace software, raising concerns about competition in one of Microsoft’s most important business segments. Anthropic introduced a suite of workplace tools, including a videoconferencing assistant, data dashboards and Claude Sheets, its spreadsheet service targeting the market dominated by Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. Several products are reportedly available in beta to paying users. The company also plans to allow enterprises to embed existing applications into Claude, potentially turning the platform into a central interface for workplace tasks rather than simply an assistant that helps users operate software. For Microsoft, this represents a competitive challenge beyond the traditional software market. Microsoft 365 Cloud generated $27.78 billion in revenue during the first quarter of fiscal 2027, ended September 30, 2026, increasing approximately 17% year-over-year and accounting for roughly 30% of total revenue. Although this figure includes commercial and consumer cloud businesses rather than Excel alone, it illustrates the importance of Microsoft’s productivity ecosystem. Microsoft’s latest quarterly results demonstrated substantial earnings growth, with net income increasing 32% year-over-year to $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, comfortably exceeding expectations, while earnings surpassed the analyst consensus of $4.27 per share. Microsoft Cloud revenue also delivered strong growth, reaching $63.9 billion, up 30% year-over-year, or 31% in constant currency. CEO Satya Nadella highlighted improvements in computing capacity, customer choice, security and cost efficiency. Nevertheless, strong earnings have not eliminated questions about infrastructure spending. Data centres, servers, networking equipment and specialised processors require substantial capital investment. Investors increasingly want evidence that cloud revenue can grow quickly enough to justify these commitments without weakening margins and free cash flow. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months which has now turned into a support zone, and climbed above $550 earlier in October but slipped toward $500 again on Monday. The price slip breached the 50 daily SMA in September which has been acting as support and we’re seeing a rebound today. The price has now pushed to a new record high above $555 area which represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MSFT buyers gave up at this zone, reversing lower. An amended filing concerning Microsoft’s relationship with Anthropic identifies at least $44.9 billion in commitments to Microsoft through June 2033, subject to contractual delivery and breach provisions. The arrangement highlights the scale of future computing demand but also raises questions about the financial commitments required to support expanding infrastructure capacity. Microsoft has a stronger balance sheet than smaller cloud providers, but elevated borrowing costs and uncertain customer spending could create problems across the sector. Concerns about debt-funded data-centre construction have intensified as investors reassess whether projected demand will justify the cost of expansion. Microsoft is also developing its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce dependence on external chip suppliers. The custom processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver substantially higher rack-scale throughput than Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually lower computing costs and improve infrastructure economics. However, development and deployment require significant investment before those efficiency gains translate into stronger profitability. Microsoft has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, although the status of those discussions remains unclear. Microsoft’s consumer businesses present a less encouraging picture. The Devices and Consumer segment generated $15.5 billion in revenue, down 3% year-over-year. Search and advertising revenue increased 12%, but Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue dropped 22%. Regulatory scrutiny is another potential challenge. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority has proposed designating Microsoft as having strategic market status in certain software markets, potentially increasing oversight of licensing, pricing and product bundling. Competition from Google Workspace and Anthropic’s expanding workplace software offering could further pressure Microsoft’s subscription business as enterprises reassess costs and alternatives. For investors, the latest reversal from $560 highlights a changing market narrative. Microsoft continues to deliver strong earnings and cloud growth, but competition, infrastructure commitments and the cost of expanding computing capacity are becoming increasingly important. The next challenge is demonstrating that its enormous investments can generate sustainable returns rather than simply supporting an increasingly expensive expansion cycle.

title: How Microsoft Missed $2 Trillion In AI - Trefis
content: Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. Think about your last big meeting. Someone opened PowerPoint. Executives spend close to 23 hours a week in meetings, a Harvard Business Review study found. For close to 40 years, Microsoft has sold that slide software. Microsoft says more than 90% of the Fortune 500 use its AI assistant, Microsoft 365 Copilot. But ask who drafts the deck today, and the answer is often an AI model. Increasingly it’s Anthropic’s Claude, which Microsoft itself now offers inside Copilot. Microsoft sells the slide. Someone else writes it. That split runs through investors’ portfolios too. In a portfolio of a few million dollars, Microsoft, Google and Nvidia usually show up several times over, in index funds, tech funds and retirement accounts. Do you know your total? A Trefis partner firm can add it up with you in a free 15-minute call. It did, earlier than almost anyone. It put $1 billion into OpenAI in July 2019 and has committed $13 billion in all. When ChatGPT launched in November 2022, Microsoft looked like AI’s big winner. What it didn’t get was the most valuable model. Anthropic, which Microsoft didn’t back until 2025, has filed to go public, and buyers are discussing a value of about $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI. The other 76% is worth about $950 billion at OpenAI’s latest price. Add Anthropic, and at least $2 trillion of AI model value sits outside Microsoft. In 2025, businesses spent more on Anthropic’s models than anyone else’s, by Menlo Ventures’ estimate: 40% of the market, against 27% for OpenAI and 21% for Google. Two years earlier OpenAI had about half. Microsoft now pays the rival: it committed up to $5 billion to Anthropic in November 2025. Microsoft beat the market.
